newsitem.title: UK: Russian star seen rising amid ratings euphoria.
newsitem.headline: Russian star seen rising amid ratings euphoria.

text.p: A trio of speculative grade debt ratings assigned to Russia on Monday places it among the best of the emerging debtor nations, fuelling investor euphoria over the future of the giant economy.

Jubiliant traders who had bought Russian debt on the rumour of quality ratings declined to sell on the fact after the major credit rating agencies -- Moody's, Standard & Poor's and IBCA -- each came in with levels high in the speculative range.
Russian dollar-denominated Vneshekonombank debt shot up four full points and domestic MinFin bonds climbed three on the news.

"It's what we expected and better than they deserved," said Kent Osband, chief strategist for emerging markets at CSFB in London. "The market has been underrating Russia for a long time and now it is coming round on track."
Philip Poole, head of east European research at ING Barings, agreed the rating was excellent news for Russia.
"These ratings put it on a par with the best of the Brady countries except Poland," he said.
Poland is the only country to have restructured its foreign debt into "Brady" bonds after the 1980s debt crisis and subsequently won the cachet of investment grade.
"The rating puts them higher than Brazil and in the neighbourhood of Mexico," said Bob Hartmann, head of east European sales at Chase Investment Bank in London.
Earlier on Monday Moody's assigned Russia's long term foreign currency debt BA2 -- two notches below investment grade.

S&P's, which economists say is often more conservative in its judgements of eastern Europe, awarded it BB minus -- three notches below investment level. It scored highest with newcomer IBCA, the European rating agency, which gave it BB plus.
Economists and traders agreed that the disparites in rating levels were less important than the uncertainty they removed from the market.
"Any rating itself is good news," Osband said. "It puts it on the map, it lets it be compared to other countries, and it sets it on the road to normalcy."
But he injected a note of caution.

"A BB rating isn't normally meant to be awarded to a country that's a heartbeat away from trouble," he said, referring to the uncertainties engendered by Russian President Boris Yeltsin's impending heart surgery, and the destabilising influence of Alexander Lebed, Russia's ambitious security chief.

"If Yeltsin were to die, events ran to new elections and Lebed came to power, you would have fiscal problems in the run up to the election and lots of bets would be off for stability in the country," another analyst added.
While the market had expected a rating in the BB range, Poole agreed Russia had done well to win so high an accolade.
"Even BB minus is very good for Russia," he said. "In technical terms they're still in default on their debt, and BB plus puts it on a par with Hungary which has never rescheduled," he said.
"None of the agencies seems to have given much weight to the country's willingness to repay, or to political risk."
But the debt markets shrugged off any lingering doubts. They powered on through the U.S. trading day showing little sign of the serious profit-taking some economists predict lies ahead.

Most players are looking ahead to the launch of Russia's debut Eurobond -- an international debt issue expected to emerge at $300 to $500 million with a three to five-year maturity, and are estimating its price based in part on the ratings levels.
But Poole for one remained cautious. "Clearly the market is very buoyant, but it only takes one piece of bad news to puncture that," he said.
